message.content:
You are an independent advocate in a planning process for a small TypeScript service at /work ("Redbourne" — a bounded rollup service for time-series samples). You did NOT propose any cheap/local option here — your job is to argue the robust, vision-aligned case at full strength, on its own merits, so a human can weigh it against a cheaper alternative someone else will propose. Read-only: do not edit files.

Background (verified facts, take as given): the service stores samples per series in `src/store.ts`'s `MemoryStore` (one sorted array bucket per series name, in a `Map<string, Sample[]>`). Today: (1) each series bucket is capped at `maxSamples` entries (an existing per-series cap), but the number of DISTINCT series (the Map's key count) has no cap at all — posting samples under 50,000 distinct series names results in the store holding all 50,000 buckets simultaneously, unbounded; (2) `MemoryStore.prune(before)` removes samples older than a cutoff, but nothing in the shipped runnable surface (`src/index.ts`) calls it more than once — `main()` ticks once at startup and exits; there is no server loop or scheduler that re-invokes it. The service has no HTTP listener wired up yet at all (`src/router.ts`'s `Router.dispatch` is called directly/synchronously by callers/tests, not from a socket).

The milestone under planning is "bound the store": make both the distinct-series cap and sample aging real. Two forks are in front of the human:

FORK A (series cap): reject/evict new series once a distinct-series cap is hit — options include (a) hard-reject new series past the cap with an error, (b) evict the least-recently-used series to make room, (c) some other admission policy.

FORK B (aging mechanism): make retention enforcement actually happen continuously — options include (a) push retention into `MemoryStore` itself so every `put()` self-prunes inline using an injected clock (no external scheduler needed), (b) build a minimal recurring scheduler/loop that calls the existing external `tick()`/`prune()` on an interval, (c) leave `prune()` external but document that whatever eventually wires up a real server must call it periodically (defer the "make it automatic" part).

Argue the ROBUST case for each fork — the option that treats this as a one-way door or as leaving a known hole in the store's core bounding guarantee (the milestone's own declared deliverable), not the cheapest option that merely "passes the local test." Be concrete: what breaks later, under what load/attack shape, if the cheap option is chosen now and the codebase grows past this milestone (e.g. an HTTP server eventually gets wired to this router, exposed to untrusted clients). Also state honestly where a cheap option is legitimately fine because the trajectory doesn't commit to more (don't overreach into gilding not implied by "bound the store").

Keep your report under 600 words: per fork, the robust recommendation, the concrete failure mode it prevents, and the one case (if any) where the cheap option is actually the correct call.

## Fork A — series cap: recommend hard-reject (a) over LRU eviction as the "cheap-but-fine" choice, and both beat doing nothing

Concretely, `MemoryStore.buckets` is a `Map<string, Sample[]>` with no cap on key count (`store.ts:11`, `put()` at line 22-33 unconditionally does `buckets.set(sample.series, bucket)` for any new name). Once an HTTP listener is wired to `Router.dispatch` (the milestone's own stated trajectory — `router.ts` is explicitly "transport-agnostic on purpose," i.e., built to have a socket bound to it later), `POST /samples` accepts a `series` string from `parseSample(line, ...)` with no series-name allowlist. An attacker (or a buggy client that includes a request ID or timestamp in the series name) can mint an unbounded number of distinct series, each only needing 1 sample to allocate a bucket. `maxPerSeries` bounds each bucket but does nothing to bound the Map itself — this is unbounded heap growth per malicious/broken request, i.e., a classic memory-exhaustion DoS, and it is exactly the hole "bound the store" is supposed to close.

The robust choice is an explicit admission policy at the cap, not silence. Between reject-hard (a) and LRU evict (b): reject-hard is actually the *safer default* here, not just the cheaper one — LRU eviction of whole series is itself a correctness hazard once real clients exist: a low-traffic but still-active series (e.g., a sensor that posts once an hour) can be silently evicted by a burst of new series names, and its subsequent `GET /summary/:series` calls will just quietly return empty results with no error signal. That's a worse failure mode than a `429`/`503` on the new-series path, which is at least legible to the caller and safe to retry with backoff. So the robust recommendation is: cap distinct series now, reject past the cap now, and leave LRU (or any smarter admission policy) as a later refinement if product needs "new series should preempt old idle ones." Shipping the milestone without any cap is the one option that is not defensible, because it leaves the declared deliverable (bound the store) unmet in the one dimension (key count) that is currently completely open.

Where cheap is fine: if there's a strong, enforced guarantee upstream that series names come from a small fixed registry (e.g., pre-provisioned sensor IDs validated by a gateway before reaching this service), the cap becomes a formality and reject-vs-evict is nearly moot. Nothing in the current code establishes that guarantee, so that caveat doesn't currently apply.

## Fork B — aging mechanism: recommend (a), self-pruning `put()` with an injected clock, over building a scheduler or deferring

The concrete failure today: `main()` in `index.ts` calls `service.tick()` exactly once (line 49) and exits (lines 57-59) — there is no loop. `prune()` (`store.ts:48-60`) is correct in isolation but is dead weight against retention unless something keeps calling it. Once a real server is wired (the stated next step), the process runs indefinitely; if retention enforcement is left as "whatever wires up the server must remember to call `tick()` periodically" (option c), that's a coupling contract living only in a comment, easily dropped by whoever writes the server bootstrap, and the failure mode is silent: nothing crashes, `maxPerSeries` still caps counts, but every series bucket just quietms into holding stale data forever past `retentionMs` since the per-series cap can mask it (as long as sample rate is low, old samples sit un-evicted well past their real-world useful window) — a slow, undetectable data-correctness bug rather than a crash, which is the worst kind to leave latent through a milestone boundary.

Option (b), a minimal external scheduler calling `tick()`/`prune()` on an interval, fixes the "does it run" problem but adds a second unbounded-growth risk: retention enforcement now runs on a timer instead of on the write path, so between ticks the store can hold `interval × ingest_rate` samples that are already past cutoff, and the interval has to be tuned against expected load — a second knob to get wrong, and a scheduler is more moving parts (start/stop lifecycle, tied to process lifetime, needs its own test double) than pushing pruning into `put()`.

Option (a) — self-pruning inline in `put()` against an injected `Clock` — is the most robust because it makes the bounding guarantee a property of the store itself, not of whoever remembers to drive it externally, and it costs almost nothing given `MemoryStore` doesn't currently take a `Clock` or `retentionMs` at all (constructor only takes `maxPerSeries`, line 14): this is a real constructor change, not a one-line tweak, but it eliminates the entire class of "someone forgot to call tick" bugs and needs no lifecycle management.

Where cheap is fine: if the milestone's own scope is genuinely "make the store bound itself" and a server is not part of this milestone, option (c) alone (external, uncalled `prune`, documented) is defensible only as a placeholder *within this milestone's local tests* — but the task explicitly says the deliverable is "aging mechanism... make retention enforcement actually happen continuously," which (c) by construction does not satisfy. So (c) doesn't meet the milestone's own bar; it's not a legitimate scope-fit answer here, unlike Fork A's registry caveat.
